Key Takeaways

  • Every paragraph needs a clear topic sentence that tells the reader what the paragraph is about — this is the single most effective organisational tool.
  • Use varied discourse markers to signal the logical relationships between your ideas and guide the reader through your argument.
  • Choose a deliberate structural pattern (build-up, problem → solution, or circular) and plan it before writing to show the examiner you are in control.

Key Takeaways

  • “Show, don’t tell” — use specific detail, action, and sensory language instead of stating emotions directly.
  • Create original similes and metaphors that are surprising but accurate. Avoid clichés the examiner has read a thousand times, and consider extending metaphors for sustained effect.
  • Engage at least two senses in every descriptive passage and use the zoom-in technique to create focus and intensity through specific, precise detail.

Key Takeaways

  • A review balances four purposes: inform, describe, evaluate, and advise. Missing any of these weakens the review.
  • Develop a distinctive voice through wit, precision, and confident opinion — the examiner wants to enjoy reading your work.
  • Match your tone and vocabulary to the specified audience and publication — audience awareness is part of the mark scheme.

Key Takeaways

  • Evaluation means judging how effectively a writer achieves their purpose — not just describing what they do.
  • Use the framework: Judgement → Evidence → Explanation → Counter-view to structure each evaluative point.
  • A balanced response that acknowledges both strengths and weaknesses demonstrates the critical thinking the examiner rewards most.

Key Takeaways

  • AO6 is worth 16 marks (40% of Component 1 Writing) — accurate, varied SPaG is not optional, it is a major marking criterion.
  • Go beyond commas and full stops: semicolons, colons, dashes, and ellipses demonstrate the “wide range of punctuation” the examiner rewards at the top bands.
  • Use a systematic 5-minute proofread (capitals, apostrophes, sentence variety, one vocabulary upgrade) to catch easy errors and push your mark up by a band.

Key Takeaways

  • 19th-century texts use longer, multi-clause sentences and elevated vocabulary — find the main clause first, then work outward to understand the detail.
  • Rhetorical conventions like antithesis, direct address, and emotive language were widely used in Victorian non-fiction — these are the same techniques you analyse in modern texts.
  • Use context to decode unfamiliar vocabulary and be aware that some words have changed meaning since the 19th century. The examiner rewards contextual understanding, not memorised definitions.
